title: Worked example: Read wave graphs
intro: Two graphs describe the same wave. Use the spatial pattern and the motion at one point to find amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and speed.

steps.title: Read the position graph
steps.text: The crests are at 0.20 m and 0.80 m. The largest displacement from equilibrium is 3.0 cm. Measure wavelength between consecutive crests, not from a crest to a trough.
steps.alt: Position graph with consecutive crests at 0.20 and 0.80 metres and amplitude 3 centimetres.

steps.title: Read and convert the period
steps.text: At one fixed point, consecutive crests arrive 150 milliseconds apart. Convert that period to seconds before using it in a calculation.
steps.alt: Time graph with consecutive crests separated by 150 milliseconds.

steps.title: Calculate frequency and speed
steps.text: Frequency counts complete cycles per second. Multiply frequency by wavelength to find how quickly the pattern travels.
steps.alt: Linked position and time graphs emphasize one complete spatial cycle and one complete time cycle.

steps.title: Check what each value means
steps.text: The wave advances one wavelength during one period. Its amplitude is 3.0 cm, while the distance from trough to crest is 6.0 cm. These are different measurements.
steps.alt: Travelling wave with separate arrows for amplitude, full crest-to-trough height, and one wavelength.

summary: Use a position graph for wavelength and a time graph for period. Read the axes before choosing an equation.
placement: Section 2: after frequency, period, and wave-speed definitions.

title: Worked example: Add overlapping pulses
intro: Two pulses overlap on a rope. At the marked point, one would displace the rope 3.0 cm upward and the other 2.0 cm downward. Find the combined displacement.

steps.title: Choose a positive direction
steps.text: Choose upward as positive. Measure both displacements from the same equilibrium line at the same position and instant.
steps.alt: Two separate pulse contributions at one marked location, upward and downward from equilibrium.

steps.title: Add the signed displacements
steps.text: The principle of superposition adds displacements, including their signs. It does not add their absolute sizes.
steps.alt: Aligned contribution bars show an upward displacement partly cancelled by a downward displacement.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.text: The positive answer places the rope 1.0 cm above equilibrium at this point. This is partial destructive interference.
steps.alt: The combined pulse lies above equilibrium at the marked point.

steps.title: Test complete cancellation
steps.text: If the downward contribution were 3.0 cm, the instantaneous displacement at the point would be zero. The pulses continue through each other; zero displacement is not proof that all wave energy vanished.
steps.alt: Signed pulse displacements are compared at the same position to illustrate superposition.

summary: Add signed displacements at the same place and time. Cancellation describes the instantaneous displacement.
placement: Section 3: directly before or after the interference interactive.

title: Worked example: Sound spreads with distance
intro: A small sound source produces an intensity of 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ W/m² at 2.0 m. Find the intensity at 6.0 m. Assume spherical spreading, with negligible absorption and reflections.

steps.title: Identify the two distances
steps.text: Compare the same source at two locations. Its power stays constant while the area over which that power spreads increases.
steps.alt: Source at the center of concentric spherical-wave cross sections, with receivers at 2 and 6 metres.

steps.title: Use the inverse-square relationship
steps.text: Intensity is power per unit area. A sphere has area proportional to the square of its radius, so intensity decreases as the square of distance increases.
steps.alt: Equal amounts of outgoing energy spread across a small and a larger spherical surface.

steps.title: Substitute and calculate
steps.text: The distance becomes three times as large. Square the distance ratio before multiplying by the starting intensity.
steps.alt: Receivers on the inner and outer wavefronts, with the outer surface divided into more equal areas.

steps.title: Check the ratio
steps.text: Tripling the distance produces one-ninth the intensity in this model. This does not mean the sound is perceived as exactly one-ninth as loud.
steps.alt: Nine equal area tiles illustrate how the same outgoing power is distributed over nine times the area.

summary: For a fixed point-like source in open space, intensity follows an inverse-square relationship. Reflections and absorption can change real measurements.
placement: Section 1: after sound intensity and distance.

title: Worked example: Design two pipes for one note
intro: Design an open pipe and a pipe closed at one end with the same 170 Hz fundamental. Use a sound speed of 340 m/s and ignore end correction.

steps.title: Draw the fundamental patterns
steps.text: These curves show air displacement. An open end is a displacement antinode; a closed end is a displacement node. The open pipe contains half a wavelength, and the stopped pipe contains a quarter.
steps.alt: Open pipe with displacement antinodes at both ends and stopped pipe with one displacement node and one antinode.

steps.title: Find the shared wavelength
steps.text: Both pipes make the same frequency in the same air. Their wavelengths therefore match even though their lengths differ.
steps.alt: Fundamental standing-wave patterns in an open pipe and a pipe closed at one end show their different required lengths.

steps.title: Calculate each length
steps.text: Use the fraction of a wavelength that fits each fundamental pattern. For the same fundamental, the stopped pipe is half as long.
steps.alt: Open pipe of 1.00 metre and stopped pipe of 0.500 metre drawn to the same length scale.

steps.title: Check the next allowed mode
steps.text: An ideal open pipe supports every positive integer harmonic. An ideal pipe closed at one end supports only odd harmonics. Its next allowed mode is the third harmonic.
steps.alt: Next displacement modes: full wavelength in the open pipe and three quarters of a wavelength in the stopped pipe.

summary: Start with the boundary conditions, then choose the wavelength-to-length relationship. Distinguish the next allowed mode from the second harmonic.
placement: Section 2: before Design the Perfect Instrument.

title: Worked example: Analyze resonance measurements
intro: A tube closed at one end resonates in its fundamental at 500 Hz with an air-column length of 17.0 cm. Find the sound speed, then analyze three trial results. Ignore end correction.

steps.title: Convert the measured length
steps.text: The fundamental of a stopped tube contains one-quarter wavelength. Convert centimetres to metres so the calculated speed will be in metres per second.
steps.alt: Ruler beside a stopped air column marks 17.0 centimetres, with a quarter-wave displacement pattern.

steps.title: Calculate the trial speed
steps.text: Use the measured wavelength and the driving frequency. This result is an estimate based on this trial.
steps.alt: Sound source drives the stopped tube while the resonant displacement pattern is highlighted.

steps.title: Average repeated trials
steps.text: Suppose three trials give speeds of 338, 340, and 342 m/s. Average the trial speeds rather than choosing only the closest result.
steps.alt: Three trial markers cluster on a speed scale around a central mean marker.

steps.title: Compare with the reference
steps.text: Using 343 m/s as the reference, divide the absolute difference by the reference value. This is percentage error or deviation from a reference, not symmetric percent difference.
steps.alt: Measured mean and reference speed shown close together on a magnified horizontal scale.

summary: Convert units, calculate each trial, average the estimates, then compare with the stated reference. Keep enough digits until the final result.

title: Worked example: From wavelength to photon energy
intro: Light in vacuum has a wavelength of 500 nm. Find its frequency and the energy of one photon. Use c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.

steps.title: Convert nanometres to metres
steps.text: The speed of light is in metres per second, so first express wavelength in metres.
steps.alt: A green wave with one wavelength bracketed and a nanometre scale.

steps.title: Calculate frequency
steps.text: Rearrange the wave-speed relationship before substituting. A shorter vacuum wavelength would correspond to a higher frequency.
steps.alt: Wave cycles pass a fixed detector; the marked wavelength and detector are emphasized.

steps.title: Calculate one photon’s energy
steps.text: Multiply frequency by Planck’s constant. The result describes one photon, not the entire light beam.
steps.alt: A single photon event is highlighted from a stream of identical green photon symbols.

steps.title: Separate photon energy from beam energy
steps.text: If twice as many photons of this wavelength arrive, the total energy doubles. The frequency and energy of each photon stay the same.
steps.alt: Two equal-time streams contain different numbers of identical-color photon symbols.

summary: Wavelength sets frequency in vacuum, and frequency sets energy per photon. Photon count also matters when comparing total beam energy.
placement: U5L3 section 1 for wave conversion; U5L5 section 1 if photon-energy calculation is introduced there.

title: Worked example: Find a real lens image
intro: A 3.0 cm tall object is 30 cm from a converging lens with focal length +20 cm. Find the image distance, magnification, and image height using the thin-lens model.

steps.title: Assign the signs
steps.text: Use a positive focal length for a converging lens and a positive object distance for this real object. The object is outside the focal point, so expect a real image.
steps.alt: Converging lens with an upright object outside the left focal point; both focal points are labeled.

steps.title: Rearrange the thin-lens equation
steps.text: Isolate the reciprocal of image distance. Keep every distance in centimetres for this calculation.
steps.alt: A parallel principal ray refracts through the far focal point, and a central ray continues straight.

steps.title: Solve for distance and size
steps.text: Take the reciprocal to obtain image distance. Then calculate magnification and multiply it by the object height.
steps.alt: Principal rays meet at an inverted image on the far side, twice the object height.

steps.title: Interpret and check
steps.text: Positive image distance means a real image on the opposite side of the lens. Negative magnification means inverted. Its magnitude of 2 means twice as tall. A screen placed at the image can capture it.
steps.alt: A screen at the real image intercepts the converging rays and displays the inverted object.

summary: The result is a real, inverted image 60 cm from the lens, with height 6.0 cm and magnification −2.0. The ray diagram and signs agree.
placement: Section 2: after ray rules, before the thin-lens application.

title: Worked example: Find a virtual lens image
intro: Move the same 3.0 cm object to 10 cm from the converging lens. Its focal length is still +20 cm. Determine how the image changes.

steps.title: Predict from the object position
steps.text: The object now lies inside the focal length. Transmitted rays diverge, so expect an upright virtual image on the object side.
steps.alt: An upright object lies between a converging lens and its near focal point.

steps.title: Solve the lens equation
steps.text: Use the same equation and sign convention as for the real image. A negative answer is meaningful, not automatically an error.
steps.alt: Outgoing rays diverge; dashed backward extensions meet on the object side.

steps.title: Calculate the magnification
steps.text: The two minus signs give positive magnification. Multiply by the object height to find the upright image height.
steps.alt: The virtual image is upright and twice the height of the object; dashed rays locate it.

steps.title: Use a physical check
steps.text: The image is virtual because the actual transmitted rays do not meet there. Moving a screen cannot capture this image. If the object were exactly at the focal point, the outgoing rays would be parallel.
steps.alt: Diverging transmitted rays and dashed backward extensions locate an upright virtual image.

summary: The virtual image is 20 cm from the lens on the object side, upright, and twice as tall. Dashed backward extensions locate it.
placement: Section 2: immediately after the real-image example.

title: Optional worked example: Calculate a refracted angle
intro: Light enters glass from air at 45.0° to the normal. Use refractive indices 1.00 for air and 1.50 for glass. Find the refracted angle.

steps.title: Measure from the normal
steps.text: The normal is perpendicular to the boundary. The incident angle is measured between the incoming ray and that normal, not along the surface.
steps.alt: Air-glass boundary with a perpendicular dashed normal and an incoming ray at 45 degrees.

steps.title: Rearrange Snell’s law
steps.text: Divide by the second refractive index to isolate the sine of the refracted angle.
steps.alt: Incident ray and normal are highlighted at the boundary, with the refracted direction left as a question.

steps.title: Calculate the angle
steps.text: Use degree mode. First calculate the sine value, then use inverse sine to recover an angle.
steps.alt: Ray bends toward the normal in glass; the smaller refracted angle is marked.

steps.title: Check the direction
steps.text: The ray enters a higher-index material, so its speed decreases and it bends toward the normal. Its frequency remains fixed by the source; its wavelength decreases.
steps.alt: Wavefronts are closer together inside glass while the ray bends toward the normal.

summary: The refracted angle is 28.1° to the normal. An answer larger than 45° would contradict the expected direction here.
placement: Section 2: optional quantitative extension after refractive index.

title: Worked example: Wavelength and signal delay
intro: Find the wavelength of a 2.4 GHz carrier. Then estimate travel time for a satellite link with two specified 35,800 km legs. Treat propagation speed as 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

steps.title: Convert the carrier frequency
steps.text: Giga means one billion. Carrier frequency tells how many electromagnetic cycles occur per second; it does not by itself tell the data rate.
steps.alt: Radio transmitter emits repeated wave cycles toward a receiver; one cycle is bracketed.

steps.title: Calculate the wavelength
steps.text: Divide propagation speed by frequency. The result is the spatial length of one carrier cycle.
steps.alt: One carrier wavelength is highlighted on a ruler between a transmitter and receiver.

steps.title: Add the path and find delay
steps.text: For this separate satellite example, the one-way ground-to-satellite-to-ground path contains both legs. Divide total path length by speed in matching units.
steps.alt: Two ground stations communicate via one satellite; each specified path leg is labeled 35,800 kilometres, not to scale.

steps.title: Check a return message
steps.text: A return message along the same route doubles this propagation time. Processing adds further delay. Changing carrier frequency alone does not change the travel time in this model.
steps.alt: The satellite relay shows outward and return paths in two colors, with a clock beside the receiver.

summary: Wavelength depends on frequency; propagation delay depends on path length and propagation speed. This specified path does not represent every satellite system.

title: Worked example: Can a photon eject an electron?
intro: A hypothetical surface has a work function of 2.00 eV. Compare 500 nm light with 700 nm light, using E ≈ 1240/λ when wavelength is in nanometres and energy is in electronvolts.

steps.title: Calculate the incident photon energy
steps.text: Use the energy of one photon. The work function is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from this surface.
steps.alt: A 500 nanometre photon approaches a metal surface with a labeled energy barrier.

steps.title: Compare energy with the threshold
steps.text: The photon has more energy than the work function. Emission is possible; the remaining energy can become electron kinetic energy.
steps.alt: Photon energy bar rises above the work-function threshold; an electron is shown at the surface.

steps.title: Find maximum kinetic energy
steps.text: Subtract the energy needed to remove the electron. This gives maximum kinetic energy, not the energy of every emitted electron.
steps.alt: An electron leaves the surface; an energy bar separates removal energy from the remaining kinetic energy.

steps.title: Test a longer wavelength
steps.text: At 700 nm, each photon has too little energy. Increasing photon flux still does not cause emission in this introductory single-photon model. The threshold depends on the material.
steps.alt: Many red photon symbols approach the surface, but each energy bar remains below the threshold.

summary: A 500 nm photon can produce an electron with up to 0.48 eV of kinetic energy here. A 700 nm photon cannot overcome this surface’s work function.
placement: Section 1: after the photoelectric evidence activity.

title: Worked example: Calculate a spectral shift
intro: A spectral line with a rest wavelength of 500 nm is observed at 505 nm. Find the fractional shift and estimate radial speed using the low-speed Doppler approximation.

steps.title: Compare observed and rest wavelengths
steps.text: The observed wavelength is longer. This is a redshift in the simple motion model. Keep both wavelengths in the same units.
steps.alt: Aligned rest and observed spectral strips show a line shifted from 500 to 505 nanometres.

steps.title: Calculate the fractional shift
steps.text: Divide the change by the rest wavelength. The nanometre units cancel, so redshift z is dimensionless.
steps.alt: Rest and observed line positions are compared against the same wavelength scale.

steps.title: Estimate radial speed
steps.text: For speeds small compared with light speed, radial speed is approximately c times z. Use c ≈ 300,000 km/s. The positive sign indicates recession in this convention.
steps.alt: Observer and source are separated by a line-of-sight arrow; the source moves away.

steps.title: Check a second spectral line
steps.text: All lines share the same fractional shift in this model. A rest line at 600 nm moves to 606 nm, not 605 nm. No detected shift would mean no detected radial motion, not necessarily no sideways motion.
steps.alt: Two pairs of spectral lines show corresponding shifts from 500 to 505 and from 600 to 606 nanometres.

summary: The source is receding at approximately 3,000 km/s along the line of sight. The approximation is appropriate for this small fractional shift.

title: Worked example: Calculate radioactive decay
intro: An isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. Start with 80 mg of that isotope and find how much parent isotope remains after 18 hours.

steps.title: Count the half-lives
steps.text: Use the same time units in the elapsed time and half-life. The result counts how many repeated halvings occur.
steps.alt: Timeline from zero to eighteen hours divided into three equal six-hour intervals.

steps.title: Apply each halving
steps.text: Each interval halves the parent isotope still present, not the original amount every time. Track the remaining parent mass.
steps.alt: Four parent-isotope population panels shrink by halves across the timeline.

steps.title: Use the compact equation
steps.text: The exponent counts half-lives. This gives the same result as the repeated-halving diagram.
steps.alt: Four population panels show the expected parent-isotope fraction halving at six-hour intervals.

steps.title: Work backward and interpret
steps.text: To reach one-eighth of the starting amount requires three halvings, so it takes 18 hours. Parent nuclei transform into products; the whole sample does not disappear. Small nucleus populations fluctuate around the expected counts.
steps.alt: Parent and daughter symbols remain in the sample; a tagged nucleus illustrates unpredictable individual decay.

summary: After 18 hours, 10 mg of the parent isotope remains. Half-life describes a statistical population pattern, not a scheduled decay time for each nucleus.
placement: Section 2: after the half-life population activity.

title: Worked example: Balance nuclear changes
intro: Use mass number A and atomic number Z to identify the products of alpha and beta-minus decay. Then connect a small rest-mass difference with released energy.

steps.title: Track alpha decay
steps.text: Uranium-238 emits an alpha particle, which contains two protons and two neutrons. Subtract 4 from mass number and 2 from atomic number to identify thorium-234.
steps.alt: Parent nucleus emits a cluster of two protons and two neutrons; daughter and alpha particle remain visible.

steps.title: Track beta-minus decay
steps.text: In carbon-14, a neutron changes into a proton while an electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted. Mass number stays 14, and atomic number rises to 7, producing nitrogen-14.
steps.alt: A neutron becomes a proton; emitted electron and antineutrino are drawn outside the nucleus.

steps.title: Check gamma emission
steps.text: An excited nucleus can emit a gamma photon without changing its proton or neutron counts. The nucleus loses excitation energy but keeps the same A and Z.
steps.alt: The same nucleus before and after emits a gamma photon; proton and neutron counts stay unchanged.

steps.title: Optional: connect mass and energy
steps.text: Optional calculation: if the combined product rest masses are 0.0200 u lower than the initial rest masses, use the mass-energy conversion. Total mass-energy is conserved.
steps.alt: An energy ledger shows lower product rest mass balanced by energy carried away.

summary: Balance mass number and charge to identify nuclear products. Nuclear energy release can accompany a decrease in total rest mass, while total mass-energy remains conserved.
placement: Section 2: after decay types; final quantitative energy step is extension material.

title: Honors worked example: Turn clock error into range error
intro: A receiver has a timing error of 0.10 microseconds. Estimate the corresponding light-travel range error, then find the timing tolerance for a 10 m range-error budget.

steps.title: Convert microseconds to seconds
steps.text: Micro means one millionth. Convert before multiplying by a propagation speed in metres per second.
steps.alt: Signal emission and reception clocks have a small highlighted timing offset.

steps.title: Calculate the range error
steps.text: A timing error changes the inferred distance by speed times time error. Use the magnitude of the timing error for the error size.
steps.alt: True receiver range and inferred range differ by a small highlighted segment.

steps.title: Solve for the allowed timing error
steps.text: Rearrange the relationship to meet a 10 m range-error budget. The clock error must be smaller than the calculated threshold to stay below the budget.
steps.alt: A narrow acceptable timing band is shown beside a larger timing-error marker.

steps.title: Compare and interpret
steps.text: The original 0.10 μs error exceeds the timing tolerance and gives three times the allowed range error. Full navigation position error also depends on satellite geometry and estimation.
steps.alt: Signal timing and the corresponding range discrepancy are shown together to connect a small clock error with a distance error.

summary: Even a small clock error can produce a substantial range error. Compare signed clock corrections first, then convert the residual timing error into a distance.
placement: Before the local honors GPS/timekeeping applications; keep separate from the five core Rise lessons.
